title: Rajaraman–Wong Delay-Oriented Clustering
hook: Two groupings cut about the same number of wires. Why can their critical-path delay differ so much?
cardText: The goal becomes the longest path delay. Each crossing between clusters adds D, and one logic node may be copied into several clusters.
description: From cut to delay: a combinational DAG, node delays, a fixed inter-cluster delay D and cluster capacity, with replication allowed; labelling and reverse recovery, keeping logic nodes and physical instances apart.
teacherFolder: module03-01-multilevel-clustering (Lab 09: Multilevel), which does not match the submitted topic

This page does not replace Multilevel, and the old multilevel path does not redirect here.
prerequisitesText: The cut and grouping ideas of Modules 02–08; this chapter switches to a **directed** circuit graph and does not reuse the five-node undirected graph.
nextText: This is the course’s last module: return to [the comparison on the home page](../../index.html#synthesis).
review: The previous seven modules all reduced the **cut**. This chapter changes the goal: the **longest delay** of a signal from input to output. The graph changes too, to a directed combinational circuit (a DAG).

objectives.text: Explain how the goal changes from “smallest cut” to “smallest largest PI→PO delay”, and work the four-node chain by hand: one crossing gives 7, two give 10.
State the RW model: a DAG, node delays δ(v), 0 on wires inside a cluster, a fixed D on wires between clusters, cluster capacity M, replication allowed.
Tell logic nodes (logicalId) from physical instances (instanceId), and explain what replication is for and what area it costs.
Compute the longest node delays Δ(x, v) and label in topological order: l(v) = max(l1, l2).
Recover clusters and instances backwards from the outputs: the candidate graph gives 8 clusters, 20 instances and output delay 8; without replication the best is 10.

State the limits: optimality holds only within the paper’s model; the candidate DAG and tie rule await the original author’s confirmation; this module’s place in the teacher’s catalogue awaits confirmation.

problem.input: A combinational DAG (no cycles), each node’s delay δ(v) and size s(v), the cluster capacity M and the inter-cluster delay D; PIs are the nodes with no inputs, POs are the outputs.
problem.output: Each node’s label l(v), the selected clusters, the physical instances and the wires between them, each PO’s arrival time and the largest delay, the replicated nodes and the total area.
problem.objective: Minimise the largest path delay from any PI to any PO.
problem.constraints: Each cluster’s total size ≤ M; wires inside a cluster add 0 delay, wires between clusters add D; every instance must have complete inputs.
problem.assumptions: Logic nodes may be replicated (the premise of the optimality result); this course’s example has δ = 1 and s = 1; ties: when l(x) + Δ(x, v) is equal, the later node in topological order comes first (a candidate assumption).
problem.stop: Labelling ends when every non-PI node is processed; recovery starts from the POs and ends when every needed cluster exists. A cyclic input is an error, with no approximation.

filmNote: The popular-science film tells delay through kitchens: a dish passes through cooks a minute each, carrying it to another kitchen costs three more minutes, and speed depends only on how often the longest route crosses the yard; a twelve-step banquet gets its earliest minutes one by one; two kitchens both need g and j, so each makes its own; working back from the dishes opens eight kitchens with twenty cooks; without copies the best is 10. The concise film covers the change from cut to delay, the RW model, Δ, the label of i (l1, l2) and the reverse recovery; the advanced film covers every label with the assumed tie rule, logic nodes versus instances, the exhaustive comparison without replication, the limits of the optimality result, and what is candidate data awaiting confirmation; the lab walkthrough, recorded from the real page, takes you through the lab and the in-browser code once. The 12-node candidate graph is reconstructed from frames of the original film and the tie rule is an assumption; it is marked “candidate” wherever it appears. Every value comes from this page’s engine.
labTitle: Chain delay, then RW labelling and recovery
labNote: Top: split the four-node chain and see how the number of crossings changes the delay. Bottom: step through labelling and recovery on the candidate DAG; change D and the capacity, and the engine recomputes.
challengeTip: Question 3 tells logic nodes from instances: an instance is written “node@root”.

mistakes.title: Thinking a small cut means a small delay
mistakes.wrong: Choose the split with the fewest wires between clusters and assume the critical path is fastest.
mistakes.why: Delay depends only on how many boundaries the longest path crosses; the total number of cut wires does not decide it.
mistakes.counter: Splitting the chain as {P,X} | {Y,O}: 1 cut wire, delay 7; as {P} | {X,Y} | {O}: 2 cut wires, delay 10. On a branching circuit, two splits with the same number of cut wires can cross the critical path a different number of times.
mistakes.fix: Compute delay per path: the sum of node delays + D × the crossings on the path, and take the largest over all PI→PO paths.

mistakes.title: Representing replication with a “node → cluster” map
mistakes.wrong: Give each node one cluster number, and write the same node into two clusters when copying.
mistakes.why: A map gives each node one cluster only; after replication one logic node has several physical instances, each with its own inputs.
mistakes.counter: In the candidate graph logic node b has 3 instances: b@b, b@d, b@e.
mistakes.fix: Keep logic nodes and instances apart: instances[{instanceId, logicalId, clusterId}] plus the instance wires, and check that every instance has complete inputs.

mistakes.title: Treating replication as free
mistakes.wrong: Copy nodes freely to shorten the delay.
mistakes.why: Every copy takes area; RW’s result is delay-optimal given replication and capacity, not area-optimal.
mistakes.counter: Candidate graph: 12 logic nodes become 20 instances, total area 20.
mistakes.fix: Report the instance count and total area; compare solutions on delay and cost together.

mistakes.title: Extending “delay-optimal” to the no-replication case
mistakes.wrong: Believing RW’s optimality still holds when replication is forbidden.
mistakes.why: The optimality proof relies on replication being allowed; without it the problem is different and the result no longer applies.
mistakes.counter: On the candidate graph with no replication and capacity 4, exhaustive search gives a best largest delay of 10, while RW with replication gives 8.
mistakes.fix: State the premises: a DAG, the node-delay model, a fixed D, capacity, replication allowed.

mistakes.title: Taking RW’s “label” for an LP label
mistakes.wrong: Thinking l(v) is the group v belongs to.
mistakes.why: RW’s label is a number: the smallest possible arrival time from the inputs to v (within the model); an LP label is a group tag.
mistakes.counter: In the candidate graph l(i) = 7 and l(k) = 8, both times.
mistakes.fix: Call it the “delay label l(v)”, and keep it apart from Module 05.

limits:
- **The optimality comes from the paper** (Rajaraman and Wong, IEEE TCAD 1995; conference version DAC 1993) and holds only within its model: a combinational DAG, node delays, 0 inside a cluster, a fixed D between clusters, a capacity constraint, and replication allowed. This course’s tests do not prove optimality; they check that the instance graph is legal and that the arrival times are computed consistently.
- **The 12-node example is a candidate reconstruction**: the figure and Δ table in the original film give 15 edges, which under the tie assumption “l descending, then reverse topological order” reproduce 8 clusters, 20 instances and output 8. The original edge list and tie rule await the original author’s confirmation; they are not data confirmed by the teacher.
- **The course mapping awaits confirmation**: Lab 09 in the teacher’s catalogue is Multilevel, and this module does not replace it.
- This implementation assumes unit sizes and adds candidates one at a time (a prefix); the packing strategy for general sizes, and the paper’s details there, need further checking.
- Replication costs area; real designs also weigh pins, power and more, which this chapter does not cover.

pythonPackage.title: In layers: evaluate delay first, then labelling and recovery
pythonPackage.md:
**Base tasks** (these three can be done on their own first):

1. `topological_order(nodes, edges)`: raise an error on a cycle.
2. `longest_node_delays(...)`: Δ[x][v].
3. `evaluate_instance_delay(...)`: instance arrival times; the chain’s 7 and 10.

**Advanced tasks**:

4. `rw_label(dag)`: label in topological order.
5. `rw_reconstruct(dag, cluster)`: work back from the POs to clusters and instances.

**Hint 1**: Δ counts v’s delay on the path but not the start x; with no path, it is None.

**Hint 2**: write instance ids as “node@root”; an input u from outside the cluster comes from “u@u”, at cost D. The checker confirms 8 clusters, 20 instances and output 8 on the candidate graph, and checks that every instance has complete inputs.

kept: The structure of the roughly 13 min 52 s long-form video: problem → delay model → DAG → the three phases of initialisation, labelling and clustering; this chapter’s concise and advanced films follow that order.
The handout’s way of explaining l1 / l2, node replication and its area cost.
The 12-node worked example (d = 1, D = 3, capacity 4): this chapter’s candidate DAG is reconstructed from the figure at 405 s and the Δ table at 438 s of that video.
The practice of listing sources and limits explicitly.
